Eisleben
EYES-lay-bun
n. (the Saxon mining town where Luther was born in 1483 and died in 1546)
German Eisleben, perhaps from a personal name with leben, an inheritance or estate; the older form is Islebia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Eisleben in the county of Mansfeld was a copper mining town, and Martin Luther was born in it on 10 November 1483, the son of a miner who had come there for work and moved the family to Mansfeld within a year. Luther came back to Eisleben in January 1546, at the end of his life and in poor health, to arbitrate a quarrel between the counts of Mansfeld over mining rights; he preached four times in St Andrew's church, settled the dispute, and died in the early hours of 18 February in a house in the town, having answered Justus Jonas that he was ready to die holding the doctrine he had taught. His body was carried to Wittenberg. Johannes Aurifaber and Jonas were with him. The dictionary records Eisleben for the symmetry, and for the thing Luther was doing when he died, which was settling a dispute about money between two Christian lords. Paul's account of his own end fits it: a fight fought, a course finished, the faith kept, and a crown laid up by a righteous judge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a course as a race and the ground run over; to finish as to complete; a crown as a reward of victory; a judge as one who decides; and to keep as to hold and preserve.

expand to see more

COURSE, n. A passing; a moving or motion forward; the ground or distance passed over; a race; career.

FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in a figurative sense; to complete; to perfect; to bring to an end.

CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by kings; a garland; reward; honorary distinction; the top of the head.

JUDGE, n. A civil officer invested with authority to hear and determine causes; one who decides any question.

KEEP, v.t. To hold; to retain in one's power or possession; to preserve; to observe or fulfil, as a promise.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

2Ti 4:8 — "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing."

Act 20:24 — "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God."

Phi 1:20 — "According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death."

Modern Corruption

Saxon copper-mining town where Luther was born in 1483 and where, having come to arbitrate a mining dispute, he died on 18 February 1546.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape Paul gives to the end of a life spent in the ministry, which is a finished assignment rather than an achievement: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). What follows is not earned by that record but given by a judge, “which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day” (2Ti 4:8).

The live temptation with a figure like Luther is hagiography, which would prefer him to die preaching a great sermon rather than arbitrating a quarrel over copper. Paul holds his own life cheap next to the errand: “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Act 20:24). And the object in either case is not the man's reputation: “Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death” (Phi 1:20). Luther died in the town he was born in, settling someone else's dispute.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek agon (G0073), a contest; Greek dromos (G1408), a course; Greek stephanos (G4735), a victor's crown; Greek megaluno (G3170), to magnify.

expand to see more

Greek agon (G0073) — a contest, a struggle; “I have fought a good fight”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

Greek dromos (G1408) — a running, a course; “I have finished my course”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

Greek stephanos (G4735) — a wreath, a crown of victory; “a crown of righteousness”, 2 Timothy 4:8.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry; “and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus”, Acts 20:24.

Greek megaluno (G3170) — to make great, to magnify; “Christ shall be magnified in my body”, Philippians 1:20.

Usage

"“I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — a finished assignment."

"“neither count I my life dear unto myself” (Act 20:24) — a life held cheap next to the errand."

"“whether it be by life, or by death” (Phi 1:20) — the object either way."
